title: Problem 1
statement_text: How large can a $(c, s)$-normal graph be?
context_text: A graph $G$ is normal if it admits a set $\mathcal{C}$ of cliques covering $V(G)$ and a set $\mathcal{S}$ of stable sets covering $V(G)$ such that every clique of $\mathcal{C}$ and every stable set of $\mathcal{S}$ have a vertex in common; $(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{S})$ is a normal cover. A graph is normal iff its complement is. Every perfect graph is normal, as is every odd cycle of length at least 9, and De Simone and Körner's conjecture that graphs with no induced $C_5$, $C_7$ or $\overline{C_7}$ are normal has been disproved. Normal graphs are closely related to graph entropy in information theory. A normal cover is $(c,s)$-normal if all its cliques have size at most $c$ and all its stable sets size at most $s$, and a graph is $(c,s)$-normal if it admits such a cover; $N(c,s)$ is the maximum number of vertices of a $(c,s)$-normal graph. The authors prove $N(c,s)\le2^{c+s}$ by a linear-algebra argument, and $N(c,c)\ge\sqrt5^{\,c}$ for $c\ge6$ (also $N(4,4)\ge25$, $N(5,5)\ge55$) by an explicit construction, so the truth is exponential, unlike the bound near $c\cdot s$ one might expect by analogy with perfect graphs. They determine $N(1,m)=m$ and the extremal graphs when $c\le2$ or $s\le2$, and prove $N(3,s)=\Theta(s^3)$. As with Ramsey numbers, the bases of the exponential upper and lower bounds differ and the exact values seem out of reach even for small $c,s$; the authors describe their results as far from conclusive. They also ask whether $N(c,s)$ is bounded by a polynomial in $s$ for every fixed $c$.

title: Open Question (normality of random graphs)
statement_text: Are random graphs $G(n,p)$ normal with high probability?
context_text: A graph $G$ is normal if it admits a set $\mathcal{C}$ of cliques covering $V(G)$ and a set $\mathcal{S}$ of stable sets covering $V(G)$ such that every clique of $\mathcal{C}$ and every stable set of $\mathcal{S}$ have a vertex in common; $(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{S})$ is a normal cover. A graph is normal iff its complement is. Every perfect graph is normal, as is every odd cycle of length at least 9, and De Simone and Körner's conjecture that graphs with no induced $C_5$, $C_7$ or $\overline{C_7}$ are normal has been disproved. Normal graphs are closely related to graph entropy in information theory. $G(n,p)$ is the Erdős–Rényi random graph, and the question asks whether $\Pr(G(n,p)\text{ is normal})\to1$ as $n\to\infty$. Partial motivation for the paper came from this question, which the authors state is still unresolved. Every normal cover of an $n$-vertex graph contains a clique or a stable set of size at least $\frac12\log_2 n$; random graphs have clique and independence number $\Theta(\log n)$. Using a random completion of their construction, the authors show that for all $n$ there are normal graphs on $n$ vertices with clique number and independence number of order $\Theta(\log n)$, comparable to random graphs.
notes: Stated in running prose without a labelled environment; explicitly flagged as unresolved by the authors.
